column4: The invented categories of consecrated livestock—bahirah, sa'ibah, wasilah, and ham—extend the section's pre-Islamic animal-and-cult setting and identify it as a fabrication against God.
Continuing the cultic shares of 6:136, this ayah reports livestock and crops reserved by claim, animals whose use was forbidden, and animals over which God's name was withheld.
The contents of certain animals' wombs are assigned to men, denied to wives, and shared if born dead; it is a precise cultic allocation of animal flesh by invented rules.

A deliberately killed game animal requires an equivalent livestock offering assessed by two just people and brought to the Kaaba, replacing chance division with measured judgment and a named destination.
The she-camel has one drinking share and the people another on a known day, a repeated animal-centered apportionment fixed in advance rather than drawn by arrows.
God says that the treasuries of all things are with Him and that He sends each down only in a known measure, locating hidden provision and its portion with God.
God sends provision in due measure because unrestricted abundance would provoke transgression; the ayah gives a reason for divinely measured shares.
God provides from an unexpected source and has set a measure for everything, directly opposing the attempt to secure one's portion through a random draw.
People are challenged for turning God's provision into lawful and forbidden portions without authorization, a boundary against humanly invented rules for food.
Those worshipped apart from God possess no provision for their worshippers, exposing the futility of seeking a material share through cult objects.
God fixes the sibling shares in the final inheritance ruling and says He makes the law clear, another explicit alternative to allocation by chance.
Alms are assigned to named recipient groups as an obligation from God, presenting communal goods as a divinely fixed distribution.
When asked about spoils, the hearers are told that they belong to God and the Messenger and must repair relations and obey, placing contested goods under revelation rather than a wager.
Public wealth is assigned to named recipients so that it does not circulate only among the rich, giving both a rule and an ethical purpose for distribution.
The people of the Garden will not be touched by nasab, marking freedom from exhaustion as the final boundary of the present command to exert oneself.
The inhabitants of the lasting abode praise God because neither toil nor weariness touches them there; nasab belongs to the journey, not its divinely granted end.
The command qumu lillahi qanitin makes standing an act performed devoutly for God, sharply distinguishing sacred posture from attendance at an erected stone.
The night worshipper alternates prostration and standing while fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the Lord's mercy, showing upright exertion directed by knowledge and hope.
The servants of the Merciful spend the night prostrating and standing for their Lord, a sustained bodily counter-image to devotion before a cult-stone.
The Prophet is forbidden ever to stand in the harmful mosque and told that a mosque founded on mindfulness is worthier for standing, making the place and object of upright worship morally decisive.
Sacrificial animals and their garlands are declared inviolable signs on the way to the Sacred House, supplying a sanctioned ritual-animal setting opposite the ansab.
The Kaaba, sacred month, sacrificial animals, and garlands are designated supports for people, identifying the divinely ordered center and objects of sacrifice.
The sacrificial offering must reach its appointed place before release from consecration, so the animal has a prescribed destination rather than an erected pagan stone.
Sacrificial animals are described as prevented from reaching their proper place, confirming that lawful offerings have a recognized destination.

Between the livestock shares of 6:136 and the invented restrictions of 6:138, the partners make killing children seem fair and thereby confuse the people's religion; it states the destructive power of the same cultic authority.
God's messenger identifies the she-camel as God's and protects her drinking share, a compressed parallel to the apportioned camel-and-water scene.
The Lord expands provision for whom He wills and measures it, locating both abundance and restriction in His knowledge rather than fortune.
Dhul-Qarnayn promises the righteous a good reward and an easy word from his command, using ease in the act of assigning a just outcome.
The person given the record in the right hand receives an easy reckoning, making ease a judged outcome rather than a lucky allotment.
Those who invent lies against God receive the portion appointed for them in the Book until death overtakes them; a fixed nasib answers their false cult claims.
The hearer is told to seek the Hereafter with what God has given while not forgetting his nasib of worldly life, joining divine gift to a bounded personal portion.
The seeker of worldly harvest is granted some of it but has no nasib in the Hereafter, showing that the lasting share turns on one's chosen aim rather than chance.
Between the God-named livestock of 22:34 and the camel sacrifice of 22:36, this ayah defines the humble worshippers as patient, prayerful, and generous from God's provision.
